subtopic: LABELLING OF CANS-CANNED FISH OR SHELLFISH

speechtext: Hon. H. F. G. BRIDGES (Minister of Fisheries) moved for leave to introduce bill No. 164, to amend the Meat and Canned Foods Act.	[DOT]

subtopic: LABELLING OF CANS-CANNED FISH OR SHELLFISH
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: LABELLING OF CANS-CANNED FISH OR SHELLFISH
speechtext:
By way of explanation I might say that this bill is composed of only two sections. The first section is to amend the Meat and Canned Foods Act so that it will no longer be compulsory for dealers to have cans of fish or shellfish labelled with the name of the place and/or province where the same are packed. The present requirement causes unnecessary hardship to assemblers who pack or buy a number of products in more than one province, in which case labels have to be made for each type of product and for
each province where it was packed. The amendment will make this no longer necessary. I might also say that the present requirement is now unnecessary, as under the regulations all cans are required to be embossed with the registered mark or number of the canneiy in which they are packed.
The second section of the bill substitutes "fish or shellfish" for the word "lobster". This change will provide statutory authority for the establishment of standards of quality and grades for canned fish or shellfish in addition to lobster if the need for such is established to the satisfaction of the governor in council.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY-PUBLICITY PERSONNEL
subtopic: CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTORS-BANFF NATIONAL PARK
speechtext:
1.	Yes.
2.	As of May 13 there were 47 postponed conscientious objectors in Banff national park.
Conscientious objectors doing alternative service work in camps receive a wage of 50 cents per day. A subforeman alternative service worker receives 75 cents a day, and a foreman alternative service worker is paid $1 per day. In addition, they are provided with board and lodging and the necessary work clothing to supplement the worker's own equipment. They are also entitled to receive benefits under the Government Employees' Compensation Act as though they were "employees" as defined by that act.
3.	Service will terminate when the alternative service regulations are revoked. An
individual alternative service worker in camp may be released any time he agrees to abide by the regulations applicable to postponed conscientious objectors outside of camps.
4.	Under the supervision of the superintendent of the park and the camp foreman.
5.	Provision has been made in the national selective service civilian regulations as amended by P.C. 2796 of April 24, 1945, section 251, s.s. (5), (6),- and (8) whereby any alternative service workers who refuse to obey an order lawfully given, or to observe the ordei'S, rules and regulations laid down for their governance, shall be guilty of an offence and liable upon summary conviction to imprisonment for a term not exceeding twelve months with or without hard labour, or to a fine of not less than $50 and not exceeding $200, or to both such imprisonment and such fine. This provision has been invoked in very few instances and only for very serious cases of complete insubordination.
6.	No fines have been paid by alternative service workers in Banff national park.
7.	No alternative service worker in camp shall go outside the boundaries of the camp as fixed by the camp foreman without the written permission of the camp foreman or other person authorized under the regulations to grant such permission.
8.	Answered by No. 7.
9.	Yes.
10.	Yes. Those postponed conscientious objectors who were below the medical standards required by the army were granted the status of postponed conscientious objectors by their mobilization boards on evidence presented by them when they appeared before the board claiming exemption from military service.
Men of low category, like any other alternative service worker, may be released from camp at any. time they agree to abide by the regulation applicable to postponed conscientious objectoi's outside of camps.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE

speechtext:
and also that the board may, with the approval of the governor in council acquire or cause to be acquired by purchase, lease, requisition or expropriation, prescribed substances and any mines, deposits or claims of prescribed substances and any works or property for production or preparation for production of, or for research or investigation with respect to, atomic energy.
He said: Recent developments in the field of atomic energy have placed Canada in a unique position among the nations of the world!, in that Canada is an important source of raw material and, as well, shares with the United States the position of having a plant able to. produce the final product from which atomic energy can be released. For that reason it is essential that legislative action be taken by parliament to control both the production of atomic energy and the materials from which this energy is derived. It is also of the first importance to encourage further research and development towards a peaceful and constructive application of atomic energy, under proper safeguards.	.
Hon. members are familiar with the .part which Canada has played in the development of the atomic bomb. The house will recall that the primary materials required for atomic fission is uranium. The Eldorado mine on Great Bear lake is the second most important deposit of uranim oxide that has been discovered to date. The importance of this material as a potential war weapon was recognized some three years ago when the government expropriated the ownership of the Eldorado mine near Great Bear lake in the northwest territories, together with its refinery located1 at Port Hope, Ontario.
Activities in the field of atomic energy have been carried on in close association with the United Kingdom and the United States. In 1942 the Montreal laboratory was established, and leading scientists of the United Kingdom joined with those of Canada to press forward the development of the science of atomic energy. In 1943 the United States had made such progress in developments leading towards the possibility of creating a successful atomic bomb that it became clear that allied efforts in this field should be coordinated and closely integrated. Accordingly a combined' policy committee representative of the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada was formed under the chairmanship of Mr. Stimson, United States Secretary of War. Other United States representatives were President Conant, of Harvard university, and1 Mr. Vannevar Bush, president of the Carnegie institute. The United
[Mr. Howe.l
Kingdom was represented by Lord Halifax and Field Marshal Sir Maitland Wilson. The Canadian membership on the committee was held by myself, as Minister of Munitions and Supply.	_
In pre-war years the United Kingdom government had made a substantial contribution to the development of atomic energy in the field of research. The joint British-Canadian laboratory in Montreal continued this work. The Montreal organization came under the administrative control of our national research council and this laboratory, with a staff of over 340, became the largest organization ever created in this country to carry out a single research project.
Prior to the war, Eldorado mine and its refinery at- Port Hope had been concerned primarily with the production of radium, with uranium as a less important by-product. Radium was in over supply at the outbreak of the war, and as a consequence the operation of the mine at Great Bear lake had been suspended. When the importance of uranium was recognized the mine was reopened and brought back into production as rapidly as possible. The refinery was enlarged and was used to refine ore from foreign sources during the period required to bring down Eldorado ore from Great Bear lake.
Since then the refinery has been in operation day and night and has processed a substantial part of the uranium requirements of the united nations. A plant for the preparation of fissionable material has been constructed at Chalk River for the purpose of exploring one particular process for producing the ultimate material. This plant has certain features that make it unique and it is believed by our partners in the United States and in the United Kingdom that Chalk River can make a substantial contribution in the field of peace-time development and use of this new source of energy.
It is expected that the plant at Chalk River will provide a centre of research in Canada which will not be excelled elsewhere in the world, for a considerable time at least.
From this brief review of war-time developments, hon. members will appreciate the important position of Canada in the field of atomic energy. I have not traversed the field in great detail, since all hon. members have in mind a comprehensive review of Canada's part in these matters made by the Prime Minister in a statement to this house on December 17, 1945, on the occasion of moving a resolution to approve the agreed declaration signed at Washington on November 15, 1945, by President Truman and Prime Ministers Attlee and Mackenzie King.

Atomic Energy Control
Atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki were largely responsible for the surrender of Japan and the sudden ending of the war. Since the ending of the war the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada have continued their cooperation, recognizing the imperative need for the control of atomic energy as a weapon of war as well as for its development in the service of mankind.
The purpose of the bill to be based on this resolution will be to encourage research in this field, both public and private, while taking adequate security measures against the use of the material from which atomic energy is derived as a weapon of war.
The three-nation declaration on atomic energy, signed at Washington on November 15, 1945, which was approved in this house on December 17, 1945, gave recognition to the need for further cooperation not only between the three countries which have been mainly concerned with this field but also for extending this cooperation to all countries throughout the united nations. The declaration recommended the setting up of a commission under the united nations to prepare recommendations on atomic energy for submission to that organization. Such a commission was set up by resolution of the general assembly of the united nations on January 24 last. Because of the special position of Canada in this field we are the only country, apart from the great powers, to be permanently represented on the commission. General McNaughton has been appointed Canadian representative, and the commission will hold its first meeting on June 14. This commission has been charged with the responsibility of inquiring into all phases of atomic energy and, in particular, of making specific proposals with regard to certain objectives which were stated in the resolution of the united nations assembly setting up the commission as follows:	(a) for extending between all nations the exchange of basic scientific information for peaceful ends; (b) for control of atomic energy to the extent necessary to ensure its use only for peaceful purposes; (c) for the elimination from national armaments of atomic weapons, and of all other, major weapons adaptable to mass desrtuction and (d) for effective safeguards, by way of inspection and other means, to protect complying states against the hazards of violations and evasions.
Much has been said and written about the form of international control that should be initiated. The government is giving earnest study to this immensely complex problem. It seems to me that the meeting of the atomic energy commission will mark only the first step on the road towards international control.
It is recognized that the final solution of the problem can be attained only by stages. In the long run the finding of a solution must depend on good will and mutual confidence among all the nations concerned.
I am sure that the house will agree with me that the immense gravity of the issue, raised by the discovery of atomic fission, and its potential danger to civilization, has made it imperative that we should approach this question in a boldly constructive manner. It may very well be that the problem of dealing with the newly-discovered force, so dangerous to human society, may afford us an opportunity of making a great step forward in the field of international cooperation.
Among the many discussions of the form which international control of atomic energy may ultimately take, the report recently published by the state department of the United States, which was prepared by a board of consultants, all specialists in the field, under the chairmanship of Doctor Lilienthal, deserves careful-study. This report constitutes perhaps the most far-reaching attempt so far *made to sketch out a plan that would control the use of atomic energy for peaceful purposes, and turn the discovery into productive channels. I feel sure than hon. members will find the Lilienthal report an absorbing and enlightening document.
Until such time as the united nations atomic energy commission has made its recommendations, and has translated these recommendations into action, it remains the responsibility of Canada, as well as that of the United States and the United Kingdom, to establish and maintain conditions under which these recommendations can be made fully effective. Canada and all other nations possessing raw materials, or productive apparatus, or special knowledge with respect to atomic energy, have a very special responsibility to establish and maintain conditions which will ensure the effective carrying out of any recommendations that may be made by the commission to provide for international control of atomic energy.
In the United Kingdom, first reading has already been given to an atomic energy bill which will empower the United Kingdom government to establish control over the production or use of atomic energy. In the United States the McMahon bill has been drafted by a special senate committee on atomic energy, and I am informed that the administration intends to conclude legislation on the domestic control of atomic energy before the adjournment of the present session of congress.
Atomic Energy Control

The house will apprciate, for the reasons I have' just outlined, the necessity for introducing a bill for the control of atomic energy in Canada, in the terms of the resolution now being considered. It remains for me to say something of the [DOT] general character of the legislation proposed. Tresh discoveries in the field of atomic energy may bring about swift developments which cannot now be foreseen precisely. Therefore, the measures for control must be not only wide, but also flexible, to meet the new situations.
The bill that will be based on this resolution will provide for a board that will continuously study the field of atomic energy. It will be the responsibility of the board to propose regulations designed to meet fresh situations as they develop. Any such regulations would be issued under the authority of the. governor in council. The board will be organized, and will function, much along the lines of the national research council. Liaison with the national research council is provided for, by making the president of the council a member of the board.
There will be provision in the bill for the incorporation of crown companies, and for the taking over of existing crown companies, should the board decide that atomic energy operations can better be performed by separate and subsidiary organizations. It is possible that the operations at Great Bear Lake, Port Hope and Chalk River, may be carried on by crown companies, under close supervision of the board. The board will report to the committee of the privy council on industrial and scientific research, to which the national research council now reports. An annual report of the board will be tabled in the House of Commons by the chairman of the committee, who, at the moment, is myself. The board will make such other reports to the committee as may be required, and will also, on the board's own initiative, report any matters which the board considers should be brought to the attention of the government. Thus, machinery is provided for the government being kept fully informed, and in a position to deal with any question relating to atomic energy which will deserve its attention, or which may be brought up in this house.
Apart from the proceeds of its operations, the work of the board, and the operation of the crown companies, will be financed by moneys voted by parliament for this specific purpose. Any regulations made by the board are to be published promptly and tabled in parliament.
It is the intention of the government to encourage scientific initiative and research directed towards finding constructive applica-
[Mr. Howe.l
tions for the use of atomic energy. Tire bill will empower the board not only to itself undertake research and investigation, but also to facilitate and finance approved research, to be carried out in our universities and elsewhere under proper safeguards.
To build up a Canadian source of raw materials the government will carry out its own prospecting and development programme, and will encourage private prospecting, even though all the materials related to the production and use of atomic energy are to be under government control at all stages.
Thus the bill will provide means for continuing the important developments that have placed Canada in the forefront of war-time developments in the field of atomic energy, as well as means for furthering and encouraging research and development in the peacetime application of atomic energy. The bill will provide also an appropriate legislative basis, both for the domestic control of this highly dangerous substance and for international measures which will need to be concerted by the united nations commission.
All hon. members will agree with regard to the need for legislation of the kind outlined in the resolution, as a means of bringing under control a newly discovered force of nature which promises great benefits to mankind when applied to peace-time uses, but which has great destructive potentials to mankind unless developed under strict government control. There can be no lack of agreement with regard to the objectives of the bill, and I feel that there will be general acceptance of its provisions.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution
before us has to do with a very important problem, namely the control of atomic energy. I am not one of those who believes that at this stage, when we do not have the details of the bill before us, we should have a lengthy debate. Obviously the opposition is always handicapped in trying to debate a subject of this kind when it has not before it the details of the bill, which the government knows all about but about which we know little. I rise at this time to say something of a more or less general character, only because of the importance to mankind of this new form of energy, and because of the need to move cautiously, sanely and wisely in deciding how to handle it.
I want to say to the minister who has moved this resolution, to the government, to the house and to the Canadian people, that in so far as the measure to be brought forward aims to control this new form of energy, to encourage research in this new field of science,

Atomic Energy Control
to encourage the use of this new energy for peaceful purposes or to prevent its use for purposes of war, we shall be strongly in favour of it.
In looking over the objectives outlined in the resolution, and listening to the minister's remarks in respect to it, I see only two points on which we shall expect further light when the bill itself is brought before us. The first of these is in respect to the second objective set out in the resolution, "the creation of corporations to carry out certain powers of the board." We shall want to hear a more detailed explanation of what is proposed before we can give unanimous approval to that provision. The other is the last objective outlined in the resolution; it has to do with the expropriation of substances and any mines, deposits or claims of prescribed substances. At the moment we have nothing before us except the general statement of the purpose of the government to set up these corporations and to make provision for expropriation. When we see the details of the bill I trust we may be able to support even these clauses, but I hesitate to do so until we have seen the bill itself.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that since less than a year ago, when the atomic bomb was brought so forcefully to our attention, we have been facing a new situation. Physical science has exceeded the development of social science. We have produced gadgets by means of which it is possible that our civilization may be destroyed before social science has discovered how men in different nation states may live together in peace. That is the major problem human society faces to-day. We see physical science so far in advance of social science that the gadgets we produce have become a danger to humanity and, in a warlike society, may result in the destruction of our whole civilization and large sections of our population.
As I said, when there is before the house a motion to go	into	the	committee of thewhole to consider a measure involving the expenditure of money, hon. members have an opportunity to	seek	information	as to thegeneral scope of the proposed legislation before it is given first reading. Later, when the bill comes before us, these general principles will be	amplified	by the	details itcontains. In his remarks the minister referred to the necessity of international control of this new source of energy. I am sure most hon. members will support that idea, but in the resolution	we	see	nothing	whatever
referring to such international control.
From the resolution now before us the purposes of the proposed bill are represented to
be as follows: to make provision for public control and supervision of the development, application and use of atomic energy, to provide (a) for the incorporation of an atomic energy control board; (b) the creation of corporations to carry out certain of the board's powers, which was only briefly touched upon by the minister; (c) the appointment of members of the board, its officers and employees, their remuneration, expenses, and so on; (d) the organization, administration and financing of these corporations, the superannuation of employees, and so on. From this outline it is apparent that a board is to be set up which is to be given wide powers, including the creation of corporations and the power of expropriation with respect to substances, mines, deposits, claims and the like.
Just how far all the matters encompassed in the proposed bill are to be removed from the practical control of parliament will not be fully clear until we have an opportunity to see the bill. From the outline given to us, however, the bill can mean either very much or very little in this respect. From the resolution on the order paper several things seem evident. First, that the measure is to provide for a very extensive degree of public ownership, development and control. For example, we are asked to make provision for what is likely to be one of the greatest state-owned developments of our time. Second, that the object of the bill is either for purposes of offence or defence, offence for or defence of Canada in cooperation with our likely associates and allies. Whatever its merit-and it has merit-it is not a measure for preventing war. The minister is not claiming that, of course, but I am pointing out that whatever else it does, it is not a matter of war prevention.
In this connection let me say that the discovery of a method by which atomic power may be released and used for the benefit of mankind unfortunately coincided with the bitterest war in history. As a result the greatest of all potential blessings is now considered as a major threat to mankind. Were the world at peace, with an assurance of continuing peace, I should stand firmly for the immediate release of all governmental controls over the development of atomic energy and for the widest restoration of the liberty of scientists of all nations to exchange knowledge, a liberty which must be restored sooner or later if we are again to march forward on the road of progress. For the moment we can all understand that this is not practicable. Canada must cooperate with those nations of whose peaceful intentions we are convinced, in all necessary measures to control the
Atomic Energy Control

development and use of atomic energy. Certainly I support warmly the plan that the use of atomic energy for military purposes must be kept the sacred prerogative of the government, and not be permitted to be left in private hands. This involves the possibility that government monopoly in this field will be automatically extended to cover those possible uses of atomic energy which are not of a destructive but rather of a constructive nature. It is quite possible rigid governmental control of the military use of atomic energy may involve hampering limitations upon the development of these peaceful uses.
It is our intention to support the government's rigid control of atomic energy development for urgent reasons of national and international safety, not because we believe that the government should retain a perpetual monopoly in this most important field, if peace were assured to us. I think all will agree that we must look forward, and not backward. We must have confidence that lasting peace will eventually be established. But that time is not here yet. For that reason I agree that this particular subject is one which must remain under most rigid government control. Whether these bodies that the government proposes to be set up will be for the purpose of developing atomic energy or for the purpose of preventing its development for destructive use, or for both, has not been made clear to us at this stage of our proceedings.
So far as this resolution goes, it looks as if the government is planning to be ready for the eventuality of war, not for the prevention of war. The defence of Canada is a perfectly laudable purpose in itself. I would point out, however, that we have nothing before us to suggest that by enacting this measure into law we are solving or even coming within a measurable distance of solving the two great problems facing us, namely, (1), the development of atomic energy for economic use and benefit, and (2) the prevention of its use for war and devastation.
At this point some more, general observations on the problem of the control of atomic energy I hope will be in order. There is a strong demand in this age to place in the hands of the government the manufacture of instruments that may be used for war. There are very few who will dispute that the manufacture of war instruments should be in the hands of the government. I agree that this is desirable if they are to continue to exist at all. But I am wondering if the dust and smoke of the bombs that landed on Hiroshima and Nagasaki are'not clouding our thinking at this hour and making it impossible for us

to appreciate the sweeping changes on the industrial front that are inherent in the fact of the atomic discovery.
The impending change in our economy may be more sweeping, in my opinion, than that following the industrial revolution. I wholly disagree with those who assert that we shall not see, the application of atomic energy for practical purposes in our lifetime. It is the viewr of many that it will revolutionize science in the fight against disease, and revolutionize the means of supplying power to the enterprises of our already complex society. As it takes its place in competition with electricity and steam, many believe-and certainly I believe-that atomic energy will bring a transformation in our capital goods structure greater than that attending the industrial revolution of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.
The difficulty is that while men and women are paralysed by the fear of the potential dangers of atomic energy, its development for peaceful purposes will be hampered. We all know that the great developments of the age of steam and of the age of electricity would not have been possible had industry been kept within the iron grip of government ownership and control. Furthermore I think the events of the last thirty years-have proved that, whatever merits there are in government ownership and control, economic power held by governments tends to place in the hands of the few who form the governments not only the control of these government-owned enterprises, but the power of decisions on matters affecting whole populations. The few who are in government have the power to decide what is good for the many. But what is more important is that the threat of this dictatorial power becomes dangerous when left in a few hands. The concentration of economic power in the hands of a dictatorial government is much more likely to lead to war than if that power be widely diffused among the people as in a true democracy.
That is one of the major arguments for democracy in this age, namely, that the decision as to peace or war is left to democratic procedure. The danger of rushing unthinkingly into war is much less than where such decision rests in the hands of only a few.
There is no use in shutting our eyes to the dangers that lie about us. Much of Europe to-day is neither peaceful nor free; much of that continent is in the grip of a totalitarian power quite as thorough, and some consider quite as ruthless, as the power that we fought for five years to destroy. The business of making competition serve the purposes of

Atomic Energy Control
progress deserves a high priority in the governments of those countries that still adhere to the democratic process.
It. will thus be seen that this generation in the democracies has a heavy responsibility. It faces a great challenge, one of the greatest of all time. Three facts stand out as never before:
1.	The devastating potentialities of atomic energy have been demonstrated. They are in the minds of everyone and, therefore, need not be elaborated again here.
2.	We have become the custodians of a new type of knowledge and of power that has more promise of good and greater of evil than any set of facts ever before placed at the disposition of mankind.
3.	We have made great strides in the physical sciences, but we have lagged behind in social science, and particularly the science of nation states living together in peace. The great advances in the physical sciences have universalized our thinking, while our social thinking in many respects still conforms more to the organization of a local community .
Obviously, something new and vastly more of understanding must be brought into the relations between communities if the homicidal danger of the atomic weapon is to be averted. The science of living together has been outdistanced by our scientific capacities for penetrating the unknown, and for producing gadgets potentially more dangerous to a society of nation states than anything we have ever known before.
I stated on another occasion that we must begin to move oat of a world of conflicting economic nationalisms and accept the world of interdependence that has become, our heritage, and that there should be no delay in making a firm beginning in that direction. The overwhelming majority of mankind of every race and in every clime craves for permanent and lasting peace. The danger is that mere handfuls of men, here and there, may still plan for national' or ideological expansion, even for war, using bogus. revolutions as the stalking horses of their aggressive designs.
It is one thing to try to control atomic energy. But our main problem is to prevent war. If we cannot make reasonably sure that we can prevent war, we should of course *take steps to make as certain as we can that this new instrument of death will not again be used in war. That means putting it into the hands of an international authority which will be given the power to issue a passport that will have to be accepted by every national state. All our vague talk of abridging sovereignty and limiting sovereignty is a mere
patter of words. War must be averted. The atomic bomb we must find a way to debar or denature. It is not by abridging and restricting and hampering national development and growth that the goal of real peace is to be achieved; it is rather by clothing an international authority with such prestige and power that we can be assured in this parliament from year to year that there are not underground, clandestine factories stealthily preparing to obliterate large sections of the human race. Until we make a firm beginning in this direction, we are but fooling the people when we pretend that legislation such as this offers as security in this very insecure age.
Pass the bill., with such amendments as may be necessary, if any. But let us not stop there. Let us either banish war or let us take practical steps with other nations to prohibit the use of the atomic bomb, in the event that another cataclysm should visit itself upon mankind.
The discovery of practical methods of producing nuclear fission has presented the human race with its most supreme challenge. Can the world of politics and law reveal comparable inventiveness and skill so that the invention may be turned to good use? It is not alone a moral problem; it is a problem of world1 organization.
The minister in his remarks referred to the work of a board of consultants in our neighbour country to the south, the chairman of which is David E. Lilienthal. The report prepared for the United States government by this board of which Mr. Lilienthal is chairman happily does somewhat narrow down the dimensions of the problem. The report says, among others, these two things (1) that uranium is and is likely for a long time to remain the only raw material from which fissionable substances can be prepared-this simplifies the problem of control of original sources; (2) that U-235, the fissionable material could be so "denatured" as to make it unusable for atomic weapons and still remain perfectly serviceable for the "non-dangerous" uses of atomic energy. To remove the "denaturant" is possible, but only at the cost of large plants and the expenditure of much time and money.
This suggests that the way to effective control lies not in what is ordinarily thought of as an international agreement in any wide sense but in the specific proposal to put the material at its source into the hands of a world monopoly. Such a world monopoly would of course be under the control of the united nations. Such a monopoly could mine uranium and experiment with it in its denatured state. National states could acquire
Atomic Energy Control

denatured material only. The problem of inspection would thus be greatly simplified. The monopoly would be a world authority; it would be a supra-national authority.
As I said at the beginning Mr. Speaker, so far as this measure aims at controlling this new source of energy at encouraging research in this new and vastly important field, and so far as it aims to make it available for purposes of peace and to prevent its use in time of war, it will have our support. We ask only for more elaboration of two sections of the resolution; namely, the one having to do with the appointment of government corporations to carry out some of these activities, and the other having to do with the confiscation of property.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regard the resolution now before the house as probably the most important resolution that has ever appeared on the order paper. I do not think anyone will dispute that when its implications are understood. Last week a resolution was moved by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) dealing with the establishment of a more comprehensive research organization. It seems to me that the two are correlated.
So far in the discussions in this house, and indeed across the country, the aspect of atomic energy that has been most emphasized is the terror of the atomic bomb, and I think it is well that the average citizen in every country should understand what a revolution was made in military tactics when the atomic bombs fell on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. But it seems to me that only the scientists have yet come to a realization of the significance of the discovery of atomic power and its potentialities for industrial uses.
I had the privilege last December of attending a meeting in New York organized by the New York Nation and attended by many of the scientists who had taken part in the Manhattan project, which was very largely responsible for the evolution of the atomic bomb. I listened there to a statement from Professor Henry DeWolf Smyth, who, as many hon. members will recall, wrote the report on the atomic bomb experiment in the New Mexico desert for the government of the United States. On the very day we were meeting in New York, on December 1, he had been appointed adviser on atomic energy to the President of the United States. I shall refer, a little later, to something he said. But one of the speeches which impressed me most was that of Doctor Leo Szilard; I have a report of it in my hand at the moment, and I shall quote a few sentences. As the minister will know, Doctor Szilard was one

of the atomic bomb scientists who formerly worked in the metallurgical laboratory of the University of Chicago. In opening his remarks he made this statement, which seared itself on my memory:
On the 3rd day of March, 1939, Doctor Walter Zinn and I performed a simple experiment on the seventh floor of the Pupin building at Columbia.
After two days of preparations, everything was ready and all we had to do was to turn a switch, lean back and watch the screen of a television tube.
If flashes of light appeared on the screen, that would mean that neutrons were emitted in the fission process of uranium, and this in turn would mean that the large scale liberation of atomic energy was just around the corner.
We turned the switch and we saw the flashes.
We watched them for a little while and then we switched everything off and went home.
That night there was very little doubt in my mind the world was headed for grief.
This crucial phenomenon was independently discovered just about the same time by Anderson and Fermi, and by Halban, Joliot and Kovarski.
They used different methods but arrived at the same conclusions, and I have, therefore, good hopes that my own plea of not guilty will receive merciful consideration in the heavenly court of justice.
That seemed to be pretty much the opinion of the men who had been engaged in the development of atomic energy and the atomic bomb. But it was not only the development of atomic energy and of the atomic bomb which seemed to worry them; it was the tremendous effect which the use of atomic power would have on the economy of the whole world. They were afraid that man had not reached the stage of development at which it would be possible for him to create the abundance flowing from the use of atomic energy, and to use that abundance for the good of all mankind.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) remarked this afternoon that perhaps this was a greater discovery than that which inaugurated the industrial revolution of about one hundred and seventy years ago-if one may date it from any particular period. I think that is true, and I would go farther and say that I agree with the scientists who were* present at the conference of which I have spoken and whose opinion was that it was the greatest discovery since man discovered the use of fire many thousands of years ago. It foreshadows, in .their opinion and in mine, such a revolution in man's way of life as is comparable only with the revolution resulting from primitive man's discovery of the use of fire. Beside it, the discoveries to which the leader of the opposition referred this afternoon in a general way-the discoveries of coking coal, the power of steam, the power loom,

Atomic Energy Control
Faraday's discoveries with respect to electricity, and the other discoveries linked with the industrial revolution-all these pale into insignificance.
It seems to me that the purpose of this resolution and our object as the parliament of this country should be to perform the task which will enable science to inaugurate a peaceful and prosperous society based upon the widespread use of this energy. As the leader of the opposition said, and I heartily concur, social science has lagged far behind physical science, and the social scientists have lagged behind the physical scientists; the physical scientists are to-day exercising greater imagination with respect to their discoveries than politicians and social scientists are exercising, and because we as politicians and social scientists have failed to relate our thinking to the discoveries of physical science, we are apt to get into a tremendous mess in the not far distant future.
I listened with a great deal of interest to what the leader of the opposition said. I agree with him that we must have international control of this form of energy. I agree with him that within our own boundaries we must have public control of this energy. But I do not agree with him that this is necessary only in so far as it relates to the making of war. I disagree wholly with that concept. I say that it must relate also to all the economic developments of peace-time; because the ownership and control of atomic energy will set the pattern of living for years to come, just as the ownership and control of the new machines at the time of the industrial revolution set the pattern of living for our own time and the period which immediately preceded it.
I know history. I know British history, perhaps, particularly well. It was a subject I taught for a good many years, and in which I specialized when I was a student. When one reads of the misery and the poverty which came upon the people of the British isles and the rest of the world following the discovery of the physical means which brought about the industrial revolution, one makes up one's mind that never again must such consequences occur in the history of any nation. The alienation of the new discoveries, the placing of them in the hands of a few people who would manipulate them for their own use, in any country, would so undermine the economy of that country that it might enslave the many to the few. Moreover, the selfish development of atomic energy for industrial purposes in any one country would upset the economy of the whole world, and that
must not be permitted to happen in 1946. It is a discovery which will set the pattern of life for years to come.
I listened to the leader of the opposition when he talked of the danger of a government exercising power over this atomic energy. He called that a dictatorship. Am I to understand that the leader of the opposition considers that in our democratic countries governments are dictatorships? Do our governments not rest in the final analysis upon the will of the people? Are they not, in theory at least, expressing the will of the people when they bring before parliament measures upon which, as representing the people of Canada, it must decide? I know of no other form of democracy as efficient and effective as the parliamentary democracies of the British commonwealth; and to suggest that in a resolution of this description, to be followed by a bill setting up corporations which will be public corporations, we are departing from democratic procedures seems to me to reveal an entire lack of knowledge of what democratic government really is. To do the opposite, to place this in the hands of various corporations, such as the Imperial Oil company, the Aluminum Company of Canada, International Nickel, or a number of other monopolies which I could name, would destroy democracy in Canada and tend to do so throughout the world.
I congratulate the minister upon this resolu-. tion. I congratulate the government upon it. I think it shows a certain amount of imagination which should demand the respect and support of every right-thinking person. The carrying into effect of the ideas which lie behind the resolution, if I apprehend them correctly, means that an attempt at least will be made to see to it that we shall be able to introduce this new form of energy and power without condemning thousands of our people to destitution, poverty and want, as the industrial revolution, over a century and a half ago, condemned hundreds of thousands in the country in which I was born. I have seen the long-time effect of it, and so have some of my hon. friends in this house. I have seen the stunted masses in the northern industrial areas, the stunted masses in the Manchester slums, in the Yorkshire mills and in the London slums.

Yes. I have seen, written on their bodies, the evil results of the industrial revolution. Therefore we dare not permit that kind of thing to happen again in the history of any country. The use of atomic energy, in our opinion, must be to benefit
Atomic Energy Control

society and not to benefit a few people in society. Its misuse would upset the economy of the world and cause untold misery, but its use for the benefit of mankind would inaugurate a new era.
Even before the war, educationists were concerned with the problem of leisure. I wonder if we realize to-day just what the problem of leisure will be when this new source of energy is developed. I agree with the leader of the opposition to this extent, that the development of atomic energy is at hand. I do not know when it will be used, but I heard certain statements made at the conference which I attended. I heard it said that in all probability within the space of five years a city the size of Seattle-that was the city named-might be heated by atomic energy. I heard it said that those who were expecting atomic energy to be used for the operation of automobiles, for example, were going to be disappointed for some time to come, because it was highly probable that what I might call the machine or the apparatus which would be necessary to utilize that atomic energy for transportation would be so large as to require perhaps a ship to carry it, and therefore the first vehicle that would utilize atomic energy might be a ship. It was said however that the time would come when the ingenuity of man would reduce the apparatus to the size where it could be used for all means of transportation, though that might be fifteen, or twenty, or twenty-five years away. But not one scientist there believed that a period of more than a quarter of a century would pass before atomic energy would be generally used throughout the world.
That is why I say that the problem of leisure forces itself upon our attention. Scientists say that a .pound of uranium, the cost of which was put in December at $3, could deliver as much energy as 1.000 tons of coal as that fuel is at present utilized. If that is so, one can understand at once what it might mean in the coal industry, in the mining industry, what it might mean in transportation. For something like forty per cent of our transportation system is engaged in the movement of such heavy freight as fuel oils, coal and so on. If that is true, one can see what effect it will have .on the entire transportation system and on the movement of heavy freight.
If we do not seek to control this energy and to plan its use to inaugurate the atomic age, we may be faced not with leisure but with technological, unemployment. Of course the only difference between leisure and unemployment is that leisure is enjoyable unemployment while unemployment is unenjoyable leisure. That is what it amounts to, and so

we dare not leave the development of this energy in private hands. From its very nature it is imperative that it be publicly owned and controlled as a public enterprise.
I remember very well some of the speeches of the former leader of the opposition, the Right Hon, R. B. Bennett, I remember sitting here and hearing him' thunder across this chamber, as was his wont, with regard to radio and the necessity for bringing that great utility under public ownership and control, and I remember too his saying to the members of the house at that time: "Who is there among us who would repeat the mistakes of the past? Who is there, among us who, if he could, would not have preserved some of the great resources of the country for the good of the nation instead of for private exploitation?"
The former leader of the opposition was a very interesting man, and in some respects a far-sighted statesman who saw some of the implications of these great new scientific discoveries, such as radio, television and so on; and were he here now I am perfectly certain he would take the same view of atomic energy'.
Of course I do not follow all the fanciful things that we are told. We are told., for instance, that one day atomic energy' may enable men to air-condition tropical cities and turn the polar regions into habitable places. I do not know whether that is so; but if it is, it is a long way .off. There are however some developments that are very close at hand, and these are the things we have to safeguard the country against if they are evil or make available to our people if they are good., and make them available in our day. Scientists are certain that what is now within sight is something which, uncontrolled, or left in private hands, will make a shattering impact on present business, present industrialism and present development, internationally as well as nationally.
Scientists, as I said at the very outset, are trying to emphasize the benefits that may accrue from atomic fission. They believe that the peaceful ..development of energy will destroy an age-old conflict, the struggle for room in which to live in this world, which struggle is so frequently at the root of war, the struggle for elbow room. This energy, they believe, if properly used will enable mankind to produce such an abundance of the necessities of life that men will not have to struggle for room in which to live, but will be enabled to enjoy the things that are made possible. Consequently, as I said a few minutes ago, the acquisition of leisure should be regarded as the means whereby we might

Atomic Energy Control
enjoy a higher cultural standard than the world, has ever known. And all this, we as average people have perhaps yet to learn.
The leader of the opposition closed his remarks with some reference to the terrors of atomic bombing. I was not here in December when the question was discussed; I was unavoidably absent. I have in my hand however a copy of an address which Professor DeWolf Smyth prepared for delivery before the conference to which I have referred. When we talk, as the leader of the opposition did, about using this energy for offence and defence, it might, be well to hear what Professor DeWolf Smyth said:	.
I do not at present see any likelihood of any adequate military defence against this new form of weapon.
He went on to say that if various devices that had been suggested were tried out they could not possibly be effective, and again I am using his own words. He says:
The nature of the atomic bomb and the speed of its approach make it highly questionable that any anti-aircraft or other defence could be developed against it which will be one hundred per cent effective. Some atomic bombs would inevitably get through.
Doctor Ivan Getting, who is regarded as one of the great radar experts of the world, and who went to London to assist in devising ways and means of meeting the flying bomb and the V-2's in the autumn of 1944, gave it as his opinion that there was no effective defence that could be foreseen against this new form of weapons. Then Professor DeWolf Smyth said also:
Since rocket bombs might be sent in a few moments from any spot on earth to any other spot, it could well prove impossible, in the event of an attack by atomic bombs, to know from which country the .attack had come.
He went on to say:
There is no scientific reason why atomic bombs cannot be shipped in trunks or boxes in peace time to key industrial and population centres and detonated at the moment desired by remote control wireless or other means.
Six or seven thousand miles away in a room a man with a set of buttons before him, with an instrument1 attuned to the bombs which had been placed in the industrial centres of the United States or of some other great country, we shall say Russia, if you like, could, by pressing the button, detonate bombs that had been planted weeks and months before, without danger of deterioration, and incidentally destroying, as one scientist said, sixteen million people in a single night.
These are the dread uses to which this new energy could be put. By the same token there are constructive uses to which it could
be put. I quite agree with the leader of the opposition and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, and I believe with all parties in the house, that the scientific development of this new discovery must be used internationally; that the scientists of the world must be encouraged to exchange information. Let us bear this in mind; there can be no blackout of science. The Germans tried it, but did not succeed. We cannot blackout science. If we cannot black it out, then the thing to do is to have an organization through which scientific knowledge can be disseminated. This means an international organization. The proper organization to set it up is, of course, the united nations organization. I do not believe that the proper organization within the united nations organization is the security council; I believe it is the social and economic council, because the emphasis has been placed in the wrong place. It has been placed upon the military uses of this new energy. I hope the great and beneficial consequences that will be felt b\' the world will be in the industrial field.
I do not wish to prolong the discussion. I wanted to express these views because my colleagues and I are supporting the resolution. We are supporting it because we believe the fundamental principles of it are sound. Of the details we may have something to say, and we may disagree with some of them, but fundamentally the resolution is sound.
At the beginning I said that this resolution is perhaps in some respects the most important that has ever been introduced into this house. The minister knows that a similar bill has been discussed in Great Britain, and that a bill very like the terms of this resolution has been introduced into the United States congress and is now being studied by a committee there. Farsighted men everywhere are aware of the uses to which this new discovery can be put; and whether in peace or in war the public of this country through its democratically elected government must exercise complete control of this great new source of energy. We dare not allow it to get into the hands of a few people who will use it for their own purposes and not for the common good.
We shall welcome the bill when it comes; we shall look into its details, and if it follows the principles of this resolution we shall support it.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): I shall not detain the house longer than a few minutes, because most of the important things which should be said have been said here this afternoon. First, let me express to the minister my feeling that- this is a timely resolution; that I appreciate his bringing it in
Atomic Energy Control

at this time and1 giving us an opportunity to discuss and consider its various provisions in preparation for the bill which will be introduced shortly.
Like the two hon. gentlemen who have already spoken, I must say that I believe it is one of the most'important measures to be brought before the house since I came to Ottawa and I hope that it will receive the most earnest consideration of all hon. members. There are many things in what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) said with which I agree, and some of necessity with which I could not agree. The same is also true of the speech of the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldiwell).
I just wish to say one or two things which have occurred to me in connection with this resolution, and which I should like to make clear. In the first place, I believe that the discovery of atomic energy has brought us to the verge of the golden age of the world. I am just wondering whether man's stupidity will keep us from passing over the threshold into the realization of that golden age. Whether or not our stupidity will prevent us will depend on how bodies of this kind react to suggestions for development and control of the energy in the best interests of the people of the world.
I should like to emphasize that I am anxious to see the best possible use made of atomic energy in the interest of peace, prosperity, health and happiness of the people of the world. That is fundamental. I believe that every thinking -man must take the same stand.
In the second place, I believe that the development of atomic energy is fraught with [DOT]such grave problems and dangers for the world that it is necessary for us to place the control of its development, at least for the time being, in the hands of the government, and I support that wholeheartedly. So far as the application of developed atomic energy to economic uses is concerned-, I am not yet just sure where that control should best be vested. I am quite content to study that question more thoroughly and to see what the future brings. But there is one thing I am certain of, namely, that Canadians, in common with the nationals of every other nation, will have to settle down to a thorough and complete study of the social sciences in an effort to find out how we can distribute the benefits that derive from such great discoveries to ail the people. All the people should share in the benefits that derive. To see that they do so we must make absolutely certain that we have a real democracy.

This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, we have heard much about a democratically elected government. I believe that we have had a form of democracy, certainly; but I cannot believe that we have really had a democracy in Canada. The reason is not hard to see. I would not worry very much about placing the control of atomic energy, for destructive purposes as well as for economic purposes, in the hands of this government, provided that I could be certain that this government was democratically elected and controlled. The only reason I feel diffident about placing such control in the hands of a central government is that under the system we call democracy the people have not yet been able to get the results they wanted from the management of their affairs. They have got just the opposite from what they wanted. Witness the bread lines; witness business recessions; witness depressions and strikes. These are anything but what the people have wanted. If there had been a real democracy; if the people had effective control of their government as the leader of the C.C.F. party suggested they have through the mechanism of this house, those things never would have taken place. I say now, sir, not only must we have a reorganization of our whole economic system in this country in order to give the people the results they want, but we must see to it that our political reorganization actually reflects the will of the people.
I am going to make this suggestion. I would not be a bit afraid of placing the control of atomic energy in the hands of the minister's commission, both for destructive purposes and for economic purposes, and its development along those lines, provided that the people in the constituencies of this country actually paid their members of parliament and actually had control over those members so that when they did not do the will of the people they could kick them in the place which was built into man to be kicked, and put others in their places. We need political reform that will give us real democracy, which we do not have under what is known as the political party machine rule which we have had in this country for so many years. If we did rehabilitate democracy; if we put new Blood into it so that the people actually did control their government, then there would be the least possible danger, even in government development, control and application of the economic phases of atomic energy.
For just a moment let me turn to the social aspects of this whole matter. I do not believe the leader of the C.C.F. party meant exactly what he said about the industrial revolution. I do not believe he meant that the industrial revolution actually caused the stunted masses.

I believe he referred to the results of the industrial revolution in displacing men with machines and perhaps another result which followed, in that labourers were exploited by the centralization of capital. I can quite understand that, but surely the industrial revolution in itself was of inestimable benefit to mankind, in essence. The whole difficulty was that we did not have sense enough properly to apply it.

So it might be with atomic energy. I believe that this is one of the greatest discoveries of all time. I believe that through its proper application for the benefit of the people of the world men can be pro. gressively released from the drudgery of the productive effort. I believe that if we organize properly, and with vision, it will be possible- for us to allocate and distribute equitably a progressively greater amount of leisure time to all Canadians. But we should have begun years ago to prepare our people for the proper use of that leisure time. In itself such leisure can be a danger to humanity if it is not used as it should be. We should have been educating- our people in the proper use of that time for the benefit of their fellowmen. The greatest play ever written, the greatest painting ever painted, the finest music ever composed, all were produced by people in their leisure time. That is the sort of thing we want to aim at in future; to give our people sufficient leisure time so that they may turn to the arts and sciences and the development of cultures in order to benefit mankind generally.
We should now adopt a sensible attitude toward the finding of means to distribute the abundance which the application of atomic energy will ensure; and I do not believe for one moment that this is an impossible thing to do. I think we are on the verge of discovering it; but let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that when we do discover it I believe that it will be the seventh great discovery of the world: how to distribute equitably among the people the abundance which can be produced through the application of forces now at our disposal, of which atomic energy is one. I hope, that as we set up the commission for the development and control of atomic energy we may also set up commissions to study the needs of the.people and the means of getting into their hands the things they will need, out of the abundance we produce. As we stand on the threshold of this golden age I believe that we should give very careful attention to that phase of the new life which is bound to come, if we ever survive some of
the difficulties which have been pictured here in connection with the application of atomic energy.
In conclusion, let me say that I am not one of those who see darkly. I am not looking into the mud with regard to atomic energy. I would rather see stars, and there are stars to be seen. There is no question about that, I would far rather leave with hon. members the thought that, as men think, so will they become. If we think constantly in terms of war and destruction, as a mass of people, then that is exactly the situation that will be brought about. If we think in terms of peace, prosperity and happiness, than we are seeing stars; we. are raising our eyes to the skies. Then men will go on to greater achievements, to higher objectives, infusing humanitarian aspects into all the things they do. I plead with hon. members to give careful consideration to all sides of this question of the development, control and application of atomic energy so that the people of this land and of the world may be happy, peaceful and prosperous.

Just before we go on to the next stage, Mr. Speaker, may I make two or three observations which have come to my mind in listening to the various hon. members who have taken part in this debate. I fear there is a great tendency to refuse to face the realities. We are in the gravest kind of danger if we make a serious mistake. I am not referring particularly to the remarks of the minister. I thought his dissertation was scientifically prepared, as we would expect it to be, and sane, not committing him to any particular policy at all. But when we begin listening to the leader of the Progressive Conservative party (Mr. Bracken) and the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell) we begin listening to doctrines which might be fraught with grave danger to the world.
May I say something about one or two matters which were talked about. It is true, as the leader of the opposition has said, that the science of living together has lagged far behind. The important thing for us to-day is to make an effort to bring our social sciences up to date. Let us develop our science of living together.
But one of the amazing things to me is that we never hear a single, solitary suggestion from the leader of the official opposition or from any of his party as to how that is to be done- no, not a single suggestion. Thus far also I have not heard one from any hon. member on the government side of the house as to how that is to be done. The assumption seems to
Atomic Energy Control

be that all one has to do is to take the power away from Canada, and from each of the national governments corresponding to that of Canada, put it into the hands of a big enough board, one that is far enough away from the control of the people, and automatically the problem will solve itself.
That is not the way things have happened in this world thus far. It is true that we must learn something about the social sciences, the science of living together. The alarming thing is that all over the world nothing is being said about that. In the spring of 1945, when we were discussing the San Francisco conference, I alone among all the members of the house rose in my place and pointed out the fact that in all the discussions leading up to the San Francisco conference there was not a single hint that any of the men discussing the problem had any idea of what on earth the fundamental cause of war was, or had any suggestion whatsoever for the removal of the cause of war. Yet they assumed that by coming together at San Francisco and building up a united nations organization, consisting of a group of men who did not know a thing about how to distribute goods in their own countries, they would be able to solve the problems of the world.

That is exactly what 1 shall endeavour to do. The advisability of having government control of atomic energy tvas discussed by both the leader of the opposition and the leader of the C.C.F. from this point of view, that only the government could be entrusted with the control of power such as that of atomic energy, because if any other body had that control it would use it for private purposes, and consequently cause disruption in the world.
It seems to me I would be perfectly in order to express some observations contrary to that idea; and that is what I propose to do. Great numbers of machines have never been allowed to come on the market, I understand, because it is feared that if they were

It is suggested that we place atomic energy power in the hands of a world monopoly. May I ask this: Who is to control the world monopoly which, it is proposed, should have control of atomic energy? This does not bear particularly on what was said by the minister, but it is a matter which was discussed freely by the speakers representing the Progressive Conservative party and the C.C.F.
Who is to control that body? The leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Low) asked that question. If the people cannot control that body by democratic means, then who is to control it? That is one of the most serious questions confronting our age. Once more we assume that somehow or another, by some sort of fatuous reasoning, all we need tq do is to get control in a body situated far enough away from us, and that body will use it all right. That is just so unreasonable and so completely out of harmony with any human experience as to impress the ordinary man as being inconceivably absurd.
What will' be the policy of such an international body? Will it know how to distribute goods? Will it use its knowledge, provided that it should have any knowledge in the distribution of goods? Will it endeavour to distribute by trade? Will it distribute by free trade or by unrestricted international trade? If it endeavours to use either of those devices, then tell us how it will overcome the disadvantage which arises from having industrial power concentrated.
In Canada, for example, the industrial power of this country is concentrated in two provinces,, which run Canada. Those two provinces do just that. They drag the other seven provinces helplessly behind them. If the whole world is put into an organization similar to the political organization of Canada,

I intend to discuss that matter at greater length by and by, when it will be more in order to do so. But I am just warning members who are talking recklessly in terms such as these. They know not what they do.

Before the resolution is passed may I ask the minister to enlarge upon three aspects of this matter? subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
The measure does not primarily concern itself with the international control of atomic energy. That is a matter with which an international forum is, dealing. Canada has its representative on the atomic energy commission of the united nations. The commission includes representatives of the great powers and certain other powers. Canada was given a special place because of its contribution to and interest in this particular problem; it was made a permanent member of the commission. Canada is represented on the commission by General McNaughton, who is surrounded by a panel of those best able to offer advice on that problem to our representative.
Atomic Energy Control

Rather the purpose of this measure is to keep the situation within Canada in such a position that the recommendations and the decisions of the international commission can be, carried out in so far as Canada is concerned. We are a source of raw material, certainly the second most important in the world, and the source of raw material will be a matter of great international consequence. Therefore it is the intention to keep strict control over raw material that is used for atomic fission.

Second, we have the industrial know-how. This at present is confined to two countries, the United States and ourselves. The knowhow is really more valuable than the science of producing the atomic energy.

speechtext: Does tire United Kingdom not have that knowledge?

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
While the United Kingdom has not as yet built a plant, I have reason to believe that that country has the knowhow that will enable it to do so.
Then we are one of the two countries which have a plant that produces the final product from which atomic energy is derived. Therefore it is important that we control not only the raw materials, but, in addition, the working processes and the finished product.
One of the difficulties concerning this product is that the material which will be used for peaceful purposes is the same material which can be used for warlike purposes. If anyone had three pounds of the material for any peaceful purpose, from the same three pounds of material a bomb could be made which would destroy all life within the city limits of Ottawa. Therefore it is not a material which can be used promiscuously. Its use for peaceful purposes must be carefully guarded at all stages, so that no one can accumulate a quantity which could be used for destructive or anti-social purposes.
That, I think, answers the first question asked by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition as to the relationship between this measure and international control. This measure simply controls the domestic scene, so that when decisions are taken in the international field Canada can fit in with those decisions.

Next my hon. friend asked about crown companies. Here again the power is permissive. One operation associated with atomie energy is at present controlled by a crown corporation, Eldorado Mining and Refining. There are two opinions as to the direction of Eldorado. One is that it should be under the national research council, and the other is that it should be under the board referred to in this measure we are now discussing. It will depend upon the view of the board when it is appointed whether it should be an operating board or simply a policy board. The board will be closely allied with the national research council in any event, and it may be the decision will be that the national research council shall do the actual operating or it may be that the board itself will be the operating body. If the board is the operating body, then in my opinion Eldorado should be placed under it. I am also rather of the opinion that Chalk river itself should be operated as a crown company, for undoubtedly, in due course, it will be buying and selling materials as well as conducting research. We are simply taking permission in the bill so that if a crown company turns out to be desirable it can be created by the board.

The project that is being carried on in Canada is not a duplication of anything that has been done heretofore; it is research into one particular method of arriving at the ultimate result.
Britain is beginning to undertake practical research into production of the material itself. Britain has been the leader in laboratory work, and she will still pursue a different line of experiment.
