speechtext:
Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction) moved the second reading of bill No. 155, respecting the operation of government companies.
He said: Mr. Speaker, since I made an extensive explanation of this bill on the resolution stage I shall reserve any further remarks until later.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is described as "An act respecting the operation of government companies.'' It is a far-reaching bill because it sets up a new plan for activities by the dominion government in peace time, sets up a plan that may very well be adopted by some or all of the provincial governments in Canada, and for that reason I suggest to the house that it merits the most thorough scrutiny. The explanatory note to the bill gives a brief summary of the reasons for its introduction. It reads:
During the war, several companies were incorporated under part I of the Companies Act. 1934, to carry out special projects. Some of these companies, such as Polymer Corporation Limited and Canadian Arsenals Limited, will continue their operations for a considerable period. It may also be desirable, where statutory authority exists, to incorporate similar companies to carry out other special projects.
That is the way in -which these companies were formed during the war, and it was a new way not used before by any dominion government. A group of individuals, in most cases civil servants, applied for the incorporation of a company, in just the same way as three or more individuals from any city in Canada might apply for such incorporation; in reality these companies formed as a result of such 63260-134J
applications were crown companies, wholly-owned by the dominion government, but having their shares held by officers of the government. That is the way in which these crown companies were formed. They were operated under the provisions of the War Measures Act and were financed out of the war appropriation; each year there would be money voted under the war appropriation bill with which to finance their operations.
We now come to the days of peace, and wi are faced with the question, what is to be done about these crown, companies? Is the government to carry on in the way in which it carried on during the war? On the resolution preceding this bill the minister explained to the house that it was proposed to retain some of these crown companies and also to form certain new ones, and it is for carrying out that purpose that bill No. 155 is now introduced.
The title of this measure is to be "The Government Companies Operation Act." I would point out to the members of the house that it is a blanket act, to provide for the operation and financing of all crown companies incorporated in the way in which these companies were incorporated during the war.
There are in the bill certain key provisions. The first important feature of the bill is this* that there is no limit to the number of crown companies that can be formed; there may be-one, there may be ten, there may be five-hundred of them. It is quite clear also that these crown companies may be set up by any minister in any one or in all of the departments. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) may have one or ten crown companies; the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) may have tfeei same number, and obviously the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) is going to have quite a few of them. They can be set up in any department of government, so that we may have each minister with a flock of crown companies, just like an old mother hen with a lot of ducklings.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Chickens, isn't it?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
No; I said ducklings. Then under bill No. 154 power is given to the national research council to procure the incorporation of crown companies. That council, too, may have a flock of ducklings.
Provision is made in the bill also that each one of these crown companies can have paid to it by way of capital up to a total of $500,000 at any one time. The company gets that amount either by loan direct from the consolidated revenue fund of Canada or by borrowing from the public under'guarantee by the dominion government. In addition to being able to get capital up to that amount of half;
Government Companies

a million dollars, provision is made that each company can construct, acquire or improve capital works up to a total of a further $500,000 in any one fiscal year. As I read the bill, this means that each company may have up to a million dollars. Then, each company is to be an agent of His Majesty; it can sue or be sued. Furthermore, each of these companies can employ whom it wishes, can pay whatever salaries it wishes, and has full control over all officers and servants. Again, each company can set up its own pension fund or its own group insurance plan, subject in those cases to the approval of the governoi general in council, but the pension funds may be all different and they may have different group insurance plans.
The other key provision to which I would refer to-night is that each company must make an annual report in such form as the minister who happens to be the mother of that particular company requires. In due course that rdport comes through the ministei to parliament; there is provision for its being Jlaid on the table of parliament within a certain number of day's after the house meets -in session.
These crown companies were a creation of the war. It is important that lion, members should realize just how it came about that we have such an institution in Canada. The minister explained it the other day; lion, members will find his explanation at page 1511 of Hansard, when he said:
Crown companies were an invention of the Department of Munitions and Supply in the [DOT]early days of the war to provide a method for carrying out duties which could only be carried 'Out with difficulty by the staff of the department. Hon. members will appreciate that, at the commencement of the war, the Department of Munitions and Supply had no staff. It was a newly-created department, and it acquired its staff by going out into the highways and byways and inducing men with high patriotic purpose, men of skill and experience, to leave tlieir civilian occupations and join the service of the government tor the period of the war.
I would point out in that connection that, now that the war is over, many of these outstanding businessmen who came into the government service, solely from patriotic motives, have gone back to their businesses and are no longer available for the operation of crown companies of this type. The minister went on to explain:
One of the inducements for adopting the crown company plan was that it permitted men with business responsibilities of their own to give a good deal of their time to the government, in executive positions associated with a form of administration with which they were wholly familiar.
There were thirty-one crown companies set up in this way during the war. They have now been or will shortly be reduced to five.
[Mr. Green.l
The minister listed on the same day the companies which were to remain; they are set out on page 1512, of Hansard as follows: Canadian Arsenals Limited, Polymer Corporation Limited, Park Steamships Limited, Wartime Housing Limited, and Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited. He said:
Of these five I anticipate that Canadian Arsenals, the Polymer Corporation and Eldorado Mining and Refining will continue as crown companies for many years to come. I also anticipate that the Park Steamships Company and Wartime Housing will be wound up within the next three or four years at the maximum.
It may be that a crown company is the best method to carry on certain types of business in peace time. For example, I am not arguing this evening that Canadian Arsenals Limited is not the proper structure to carry on the manufacture of weapons in Canada. That may be true also of the Eldorado company, because it has to deal with uranium and, as every hon. member knows, uranium is of world-shaking importance at the present time. There may be reasons why the Polymer Corporation should be a crown company; I am not arguing this evening either that it should or should not be. But I suggest to the minister and to the members of the house that where we need a crown company it should be set up by means of an individual bill brought into this house to deal with that one company alone. If that were done, parliament and the Canadian people would know exactly why a crown company is required. Parliament would be able to approve or disapprove the powers which it is supposed to give to the company. Parliament could provide for the operation of the company. That has been done in certain cases, for example with War Assets Corporation. I believe that if that were the policy followed, each company being set up by an individual bill, there would be far fewer crown companies, and surely crown companies should be the exception rather than the rule. But this bill No. 155 is a blanket bill; we as members of the Progressive Conservative party have serious objections to some of the terms of that bill, and because of those objections cannot support it.
I am going to list six objections. No doubt there are others. I think each one. of these six is important, and I would ask hon. members on all sides of the house to give careful consideration to them.
The first objection is that there is no limit to the number of crown companies which can be set up; further, that any department can set them up.
The second objection is that government activities of this type are far removed from parliamentary control; the crown company is

Government Companies
far removed from parliamentary control. If this bill is carried it will weaken parliament; it will be one more step in taking away parliament's powers. The only check on a crown company that the minister can promise is that its accounts will be brought in once a year and laid on the table of the house. It may be that they will be studied by a special committee, but I submit to hon. members that that is an ineffective control; it means locking the stable door after the horse has gone.
As the number of crown companies increases, the effectiveness even of that control will diminish accordingly. Just consider the position if we have fifty of these crown companies; parliament will have no effective control over them or their operations. I do not think anyone in this house will contend that parliament has had any effective control over crown companies during the war. Certainly in my experience there has been little control over the activities of these companies; with other problems pressing, and in the hurry of the war, parliament did not bother very much about how these crown companies were carrying on.
The third objection is that no provision is made for these crown companies to pay any taxes municipal, provincial or federal. The Minister of Reconstruction pointed out the other day that a crown company did not have to pay taxes because it had the protection of the British North America Act. Hon. members will find in section 25 of that act the following:
No lands or property belonging to Canada or any province shall be liable to taxation.
The time has long since passed when the dominion should shelter behind that provision of the British North America Act at the expense of the municipalities. Certainly these crown companies should pay municipal taxes. I suppose there are dozens of municipalities across Canada losing out because the dominion pays no taxes. I have here a resolution passed a few months ago by the city council of my home city of Vancouver which sums up the situation as it applies in every municipality in Canada in which there is any considerable amount of crown property:
That this council reiterates its stand of June 12, 1945. when it passed and asked His Worship to present to the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities the subjoined resolution which was adopted at the 8th annual conference of that body for submission to the federal and provincial governments.
Whereas under the British North America Act, 1867, the property of the crown (whether dominion or provincial) is not subject to municipal taxation;
And whereas at the time the act was passed only a few properties belonged to the crown, such as post offices, court houses, penitentiaries, etc.;	_	_
And whereas since that time, and particularly during the war years, both governments have
vastly increased their holdings and have embarked upon many forms of commercial business never contemplated in 1867;
And whereas municipalities are required to provide services for government buildings, such as roads, fire protection, police protection, sewer facilities, etc.;
And whereas it may be expected for some years that the number of government properties in the municipalities will not diminish;
Therefore be it resolved that this conference reiterate its stand that some measure of relief for the municipalities must be worked out, and that pending such an amendment to the British North America Act as will require the government to pay taxes in the ordinary way provision be made by way of grants or otherwise to offset the value of the services contributed to them as aforesaid.
In that city there is dominion government property assessed at over $15,000,000 and provincial government property assessed at over $3,000,000, to a total of $18,464,150. If that were taxable at the ordinary rate that a ratepayer has to pay it would yield $608,574 per annum. In my opinion the dominion has been getting away with murder in the last few years in so far as exemption from payment of municipal taxes is concerned. Also, the crown companies pay no provincial taxes, nor do they pay federal taxes and therefore are not on the same footing as private business, and that brings me to my fourth objection.
In some cases crown companies will be in direct competition with private business. I do not think any member of the house can question that fact. They are bound to be in competition with private business, to some degree at least, and one proof of that fact is that these crown companies are set up in the way that has been devised so that they can pay the same type of salaries that are paid by private industry. I do not want hon. members to think I am speaking on behalf of big business, because the big fellow is usually able to take care of himself. It is the little fellow who goes to the wall and who will suffer from competition of this type. It should be made clear to every Canadian that with each independent business man destroyed we chop down one of the pillars on which the nation rests.
The fifth objection is that the bill makes possible the setting up of a super civil service. Employment is entirely in the hands of officers of the crown companies. They can hire whomsoever they choose and pay whatever salaries they wish. The minister explained that one of the reasons he wanted crown companies was to pay salaries commensurate with those paid by private industry. These provisions regarding employment leave the way wide open for patronage, wide open for employment of supporters of the government
Government Companies

that happens to be in power at the time. The companies are designed to get around the Civil Service Act. That is one reason for having them.
The Civil Service Act, as hon. members know, is based upon the principle of employment on merit; upon the principle of everyone having the same type of pension plan and of keeping appointments entirely away from patronage. But these crown companies are set up in such a way that their employees can become a super civil service.
The sixth objection is that by using these crown companies the government is putting into effecet a very fine method of bringing about a socialist state. There are "hear, hears" from my left.' The members of the C.C.F. party will agree, I am sure, with that statement; and that very fact should be a warning to the private members on the Liberal side of the house. Let that sink in, that the C.C.F. are applauding the fact that this bill makes socialism easy. They have already been using this same system in the province of Saskatchewan and naturally they want the same system written into the federal law. I warn the government, I warn private members of the Liberal party particularly, that this bill-

speechtext: We are stealing their thunder.

to seeing a crown corporation set up. Crown corporations have their place, and that was amply demonstrated during the time of emergency in the war. I have never objected to Polymer; I have never objected to Canadian Arsenals, and I have never objected to any other crown companies being set up to meet an emergency situation. But I claim that the emergency situation requiring them has largely passed. We are now facing a time of peace, and certainly it is only right that we should return in our rehabilitation and reconstruction measures so far as we possibly can to the system of enterprise carried on privately. I have never criticized those crown corporations; but, sir, why we should now give blanket powers to the government to set up other corporations at will and clothe them with unusual powers is beyond me. The wisest thing to do, if we need other crown corporations, is to bring a bill into this parliament for each, and let the representatives of the people judge whether the corporation proposed is a good one. Let the representatives find out from their people whether they want more corporations, and let them say whether or not the minister is entitled to have such crown corporations. If that is done, and if I am convinced that the corporation proposed is a good one, I will certainly support a bill brought in to create it, but I do request that we give careful consideration to a principle which I think is objectionable, of granting the government blanket powers to set up any crown corporation they see fit at any time. Therefore, if we are changing our way of doing business, it is fair that the people should have a good look at what we are doing while we are doing it. I come now to a point made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I wish I were as highland as he is; I am only a poor diluted highlander, about twenty-five per cent genuine: were I 100 per cent I feel that I might amount to something. All we highlanders are more or less sentimental. I think the Minister of Veterans Affairs is a real sentimentalist; I love him for it but I do not follow him for

the Minister's bill and that a great many hon. members opposite feel about this bill very much as we do but they will not have any more to say about it than I have, indeed not nearly as much, because they will not have the-chance to say anything about it at all.
During the war the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply exercised great powers; We approved that; we could not be finicky about giving power in war time. At such; a time one expects a relaxing of ordinary restrictions. But now we are in peace time,, and we are really being asked in time of peace to accept a condition applicable only in time of war. I submit-and I think this is the point which the hon. member for Vancouver South made in connection with the bill-that if the measure passes we can have government companies by the score, and let no one imagine that measures creating them are going to be considered by parliament.
I expect they will not even' be considered by the government. I assume what will happen is that each particular minister will decide what company he wants and will come with his proposal to the cabinet and the thing will be approved.
Therefore what do we have? If we approve this bill we have a movement into socialism, to an extent which nobody can measures That is the reason why hon. gentlemen to the-left of us approve-quite naturally-the bill. There is no stopping place; nobody can tell us where the thing will end.
One further remark. I have made the point that people are entitled to "stop, look and listen" when the way of life which they have approved is being changed. It is perfectly proper to ask that this thing should be taken* step by step. When there is an industry" which the government thinks should be run' by the public, very well; let them come and tell us all about it; let us discuss it; let the people of Canada know what is going to be done; let parliament consider the matter, and let it be approved by the people's representatives. We are not saying that there should be no public ownership. The hon. member for Vancouver South said exactly the opposite.
One further point. There have been many references in this house to the present British government, and I submit that it is of some interest to us to know that the present British government is dealing with this matter, as I understand, in exactly the way that we propose that it should be dealt with. Take the steel; industry. They are passing a special bill in that regard and they are doing it cautiously. The British minister in introducing that measure said that the British government, proposed:
... to review the field-

That is exactly what we would do were we on that side of the house. But the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is proposing this, in my opinion, on the basis of his war experience. There is one thing that perhaps the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is not forgetting, that no hon. member should forget and that certainly the Canadian people will not forget. When this war broke out; when Britain had her back to the wall, the country about which the Tory party seems to be so anxious; when the free enterprise system was called upon to produce for war the very minister who is introducing this bill tried to let war contracts in this country for the production of the necessary materials of war to assist Britain. But at that time there was a profits limitation of five per cent in those contracts; and a statute passed by this house during the short session of 1939 had to be repealed by order in council at the instance of the present minister because for months he could not get the free enterprisers

across this country to accept a single contract to produce munitions of war to enable Britain to build a jumping off place for the rest of the world when it was ready to fight. Now, in the days of peace, he is finding himself in the same position. With thousands of our boys coming back; with thousands of our *war workers being relegated back to the streets, w'e find the free enterprisers back in the saddle putting up a fight for the removal of controls, for the removal of the excess profits tax, wanting to throw the field _ wide open or threatening to go on a sit-down strike and not produce. In my opinion that is true in every industry in this country. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is not asking the house for power to socialize or nationalize anything in this country. He is merely asking us for authority, to give him the right to act where free enterprise has failed to develop the resources of this country as it is doing in the maritime provinces from end to end. There are many small industries which could be set up there. But they would be competing with the big industries in central Canada. They are not set up, with the result that in the maritime provinces to-day you have either to get a policy of taking the people out or to give someqne authority to develop small industries in that end of the country.
That is the idea behind what is being done by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply at this time. So far as I am concerned, this bill is limited in its powers. All we have to do is to stop and examine for a minute the whole problem on the basis of common sense. Is the fuel industry in'this country operating to capacity, or in the best interests of the people of Canada? It is not. We face an emergency, a crisis, in that industry to-day. Is that not also true in the lumbering industry? People in this country are crying for houses, and we find the lumbering industry-the essential industry in the building of houses-tied up under your system of free enterprise.
We can go right along and find the same thing in the textile industry. You cannot buy a shirt or a suit of clothes without a priority ticket. The whole machinery is tied up under the system we have to-day. There is no competition; there is no threat to them. Mr. Speaker, before making special reference to certain sections of the minister's speech delivered on May 14, may I refer to one or two statements made in the debate to-night?
In the nineteenth parliament we had an overflow of government members into the opposition side of the house. It becomes completely obvious to-night that in this twentieth parliament the picture is entirely reversed, because now we have the C.C.F. both here on this side and an overflow of C.C.F.-ers to your right, Mr. Speaker.
During his early remarks the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) referred to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) as one who was riding two horses on this particular subject, namely, public ownership and private enterprise, and he also tied in the Conservative party with that assertion. I should like to ask the hon. member for Cape Breton South how many horses he is riding. I heard the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) say that in order to accomplish certain results which he believes essential to the welfare of the people of Canada we must socialize the means of life; yet if he used that expression in some parts of Canada the C.C.F. there would become furious because they realize that it is politically wise in certain parts of this country to exclude many things from their programme of socialization, and one of the things they exclude is certainly enterprises which produce the means of livelihood.
I should like to ask the hon. member for Cape Breton South and other members of his party this question: Is it the specific function of industry to provide employment? Or is it the specific function of industry to provide the goods and services which the people of the country require? We hear from time to time a great deal said about that very subject. We are presumed to have a quarter of a million people unemployed in this country to-day. Since we are' living under the present arrangement of things unemployment means no income and therefore a desperate situation, and having that situation, it is asserted by my hon. friends to my immediate right that the responsibility for it rests entirely upon the industrial enterprise of the country. In other words, they say: "regardless of all other circumstances, industry must absorb those who are unemployed." I still look upon industry as that section of our economy which is charged primarily with the production of goods and services of the best possible quality at the lowest possible price. We must recognize the technological fact that almost daily we are improving and increasing our ways and means of production. We must

Government Companies
recognize, therefore, that the tendency in the industrial life of our country is to remove persons from the field of so-called work. This afternoon the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) referred to the leisured state, and I think he got reasonably close to the conception which I hold, namely, that if we can, through improvements in science and technology, remove men from the drudgery of eight to ten hours' work a day, then that should be our objective. But let me emphasize that we must make certain that those who are displaced as a consequence of scientific and technological development are not going to be deprived of an effective claim against the production of our industrial life.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South referred to the era of peace and at the same time he referred slightingly to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). I have never witnessed the hon. member for Cape Breton South making a substantial contribution towards the peace of this country. In fact, I sometimes think he and some of his associates thrive upon the discontent of the country, and I sometimes think they are hopeful that people will become more discontented rather than more peaceful. They refer to certain practices which have developed in industry and to the report of the price spreads commission. I know all about that report. Those practices constituted an abuse of capital, and I admit that governments should have sufficient intestinal fortitude to step in and check abuses in industry which are nefarious in character. I think everybody realizes that no government whatsoever has any right to close its eyes completely to the abuses of some of the larger corporations, while concentrating upon probably minor offences which are more easily visible.
May I refer to the speech delivered by the Minister of Reconstruction and) Supply (Mr. Howe) on May 14. I would be remiss in my duty if I were not to associate myself with the hon. member for Peace River in condemning the introduction of this new principle which the minister referred to on page 1511 of Hansard of allowing crown corporations to use their operating revenues to pay their operating costs. Within the last day or two I have had a number of complaints from my part of the country with respect to that aspect of the government's proposals. At the bottom of page 1511 of Hansard the minister classified these crown corporations in three groups. First, he referred to those of an administrative and supervisory nature. He said :
It did not directly operate plants, but it supervised their building, arranged for the operation of the plants, and handled the sale of the product.
While that applied1 during the war, it is assumed that the minister gave it as one of three functions which one or all of these crown corporations might discharge after the war. But I say to him that it does not require a crown corporation in order that building may be engaged in throughout the country. It does not require crown corporation to operate any industry efficiently; in fact, of all the examples of industry I have seen, some of the most inefficient were labelled as crown corporations. Let me assure the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, that the fact that before the war industry experienced difficulty in selling its products was not because a substantial portion of our industry was owned privately. Let me emphasize this fact: whether a corporation is privately owned or publicly owned you must have in the hands of your people an effective claim against its production. We realize that we have had and still have crown-operated corporations in this country, but their products and their services are not a bit easier to secure than the products and the services rendered by private companies.
Just before leaving No. 1, let me say again that our view is that the affairs of this country should be so regulated that we shall have in the hands of our people an effective claim against goods, and then it will take no crown corporation to see that such goods are properly distributed.
On page 1511 of Hansard the minister asserted:
In the second class were the manufacturing companies. We found as the war proceeded that it was necessary to increase the manufacture of certain products beyond the capacity of private industry. . .
We agree that the urgent demands of war made that course of action necessary. But what does the minister advance as the reason for a crown corporation to function after the war? I reflect back on that period from 1930 to 1939. No one will say that the industry 6f this country was then incapable of producing the requirements of the Canadian people. I well recall that our stores and warehouses were jammed with commodities. The government of the day called them "surpluses". But we realize that the whole problem was lack of effective demand for those goods. We shall have no difficulty in securing the vast quantities of produce necessary for the requirements of our people, provided that our people are in possession of those incomes which alone

create effective demand and which alone guarantee the full-time operation of those industries.
I move to No. 3. The minister stated:
Then there was the third class of companies, companies engaged in merchandising certain raw materials and in providing stockpiles sufficient to assure adequate supplies for war and civilian purposes.
Once again I agree that during the war this was an important function of a crown corporation. But do you remember the stockpiles we had before the war, stockpiles of grain, called "surplus", stockpiles of almost every other type of produce, called "surpluses". Why, they were even paying people not to produce, in order to reduce their stockpiles. Yet we accuse private industry-at least some people do -of not being capable of producing the requirements of our people.

With the crown companies as proposed in the terms of this bill, it would appear to me that, wherever they might be located, if there is a profit resulting from their operation it will find its way into the coffers of the central administration. Hon. members may say that is where it should go. I have no doubt that, in the main, municipalities throughout Ontario and the whole dominion would bid for one of these companies if they could get them to locate in their midst. Nevertheless it seems to me that the time has arrived when the government should give consideration to a local levy of taxation of crown companies; and if we can accept what the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) said to-night, the government will in due time, and I think should, give such consideration. If that is done, then I

Government Companies
feel our position with respect to the quotation given by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) would not be very different from what he quoted from the Right Hon. Winston Churchill. If the suggestion of the Minister of Labour is acted on, then we shall be in a position to make private enterprise and public ownership work side by side.
At the moment I cannot accept the principle that a crown corporation should escape its share of municipal taxation. Many hon. members know that my background is one of municipal government. There we are charged with the responsibility of raising sizeable sums to carry on the administration of local municipalities. All the municipalities of Ontario, being creatures of the provincial government, legislate or work within the terms of the authority laid down by the provincial legislature; therefore their field of taxation is one of direct taxes, and it is limited and must be borne by the property owners.
My objection is-and I am more impressed when I listened to the round of applause emanating from the quarter occupied by the C.C.F. socialist group, that this can easily be; in saying this I am not doubting in any sense the sincerity of the present incumbent of the ministerial post of reconstruction; I think that generally we have considerable confidence in the man who is charged with that responsibility at present-that he is not the one who is going to carry on forever. This legislation could become, in the hands of those who would seek to use it for a purpose it was never intended, in the mind of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe), a dangerous thing. We are all individuals; we think as individuals; we act as individuals, and we shall continue to do so until there is mass regulation and regimentation. In order to bring that about there will have to be instituted a system of government similar to that which we destroyed or hoped we had destroyed in central Europe. I agree in that sense with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) that the thing we thought we fought the war for was to destroy state or national socialism which was rampant in Germany. It was brought about by what we might do here unconsciously in this sense.
There is more than one way to bring about state socialism. The first way. is to listen to its being advocated from a public platform. The other way is to continue to impose taxation until you have taxed private enterprise out of existence or destroyed the will of the people and their ambition and desire to make their contribution to the state. As I look back and think of the contribution which has been made by government agencies during the war-and
all of them are praiseworthy-I am still reminded that in association with the contribution were the tremendous resources of this nation which have been built up under the finest system in the world so far as I am concerned, namely, private enterprise. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the functions of government can quite properly be considered as legislative and not entirely regulatory or administrative. In other words, if there is anything wrong with private enterprise; if there may be so-called' monopolies; if some have usurped the privileges of citizenship and have sought to exploit the nation for the benefit of a privileged few, then I say this parliament or any other parliament having authority can legislate and regulate in order that private enterprise may be brought within the scope of the legislation and required to render an account of their stewardship which must indeed, after all, bear some semblance to fair play. I am inclined to accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), with due deference to my good friend the Minister of Veterans Affairs that there is something in this legislation delegating to the government an authority which, if I understand the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply aright, he is not seeking; and that is one very good reason why the bill should be further considered.
Then the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum) spoke about General Motors in the city of Regina receiving some advantage by way of freedom from taxation. In Ontario the only bonus or consideration we can give a prospective industry is a fixed assessment. Of course, if the statutes of Saskatchewan provide that an industry may be brought to Regina where it will pay no taxes, that inducement must have been approved by the ratepayers of that city. They may have taken a long-range view, knowing that at some time, sooner or later, that enterprise would pay taxes in the municipality, and that would be offered as an inducement to have it locate there. The moment we approve the establishment of crown companies, which will be located in municipalities across this country without being subject to taxation, then I say the situation is entirely different from that of offering a bonus or some similar inducement to private enterprise, since they will never pay taxes.
The real source of security, after all, is employment, and I will go so far as to say that I believe this country of ours offers everyone the right to earn a living at a fair rate of pay for a fair day's work. But I certainly do not feel that we should subscribe to the false theory which I believe is all too
Government Companies

prevalent in these days, that the country owes a man a living. I cannot accept that, nor do I think it is good for the nation. There is a tendency at the present time for people to lean upon others, and we find a constant trend toward paternalism on the part of the government. We are now to have crown companies, and we shall have no way of knowing whether or not they are efficiently operated, because we have no yardstick with which to measure them since they pay no taxes. I have heard it said in this house, for instance, that T.C.A. had an operating surplus, but unless we know what they paid in taxes for the use of airports and other property it is difficult indeed to determine if they are efficiently managed. In order to determine the measure of efficiency we must have some means of comparison. The setting up of crown companies may be the thin end of the wedge, so that our people will be still further robbed of their initiative and their desire to build Canada into a great nation. We have in Canada what it takes to make a great country, but what we need more than anything else is good, sound business management. We need balanced budgets and lower taxes, because at present our people are being discouraged by taxation, and that may account to some extent for the constant migration from this country to the United States.
It has been stated in this house to-night that in many enterprises the crown can give leadership, and I would point to one outstanding example in that connection. In the great province of Alberta there is a wealth of coal, a great deal of which may be needed in this country before next spring comes around. I hope the government are considering giving leadership in that development, because I believe great quantities of this coal could be made available. I have no doubt that one of the reasons back of the introduction of this legislation is atomic energy, which has been referred to this evening; and I feel that for whatever the government may have done or may do by way of research in this connection they should be commended, because in atomic energy we have a latent power greater than anything mankind has ever conceived. Man has now discovered a means of harnessing this power; but how is he going to use it? In the beginning I believe it is in good hands when it is under the control of the crown. We should seek constantly to see that it is developed and devoted to useful purposes. As my leader (Mr. Bracken) said this afternoon, it should not be developed in anticipation of destruction but for purposes of construction. It may be that these crown companies are to be set up in order to develop atomic energy still farther, perhaps to utilize

the products resulting therefrom or even to use the power that may be developed in this way. But I believe the minister should accept in good faith the suggestion that has been made from this side of the house. I would not want in any way to appear belligerent about this. I rose to speak only because I have been long associated with public ownership ventures in Ontario, and I would not want my position to be misunderstood or misinterpreted. I am in favour of public ownership, but by the same token I am in favour of every enterprise and every individual bearing a fair share of the cost of government, because that can become a terrific burden.
We in Ontario realize that our hydro system, owned by the crown, has brought us cheap power and has assisted in our industrial development. Nevertheless, to get a true picture of the value of such great institutions I feel they should bear their fair share of the cost of local government within the municipalities. I believe we should give careful consideration to all these matter before we travel too far along the road to socialism. Mind you, socialism is nothing new. If time and Mr. Speaker would permit I could trace socialism back for hundreds of years, and show that it has always destroyed the civilization of its day. It may do the same thing again unless we are alive to what it really means, and unless we decide whether we are to have our people reduced to a point where they are subservient to the government, or whether the government is to remain the servant of the people. So that to-night I am simply trying to place myself on record as believing in public owmership. I am also in favour of a limited development in the matter of crown companies, as long as certain protection is given and the right of taxation is admitted. If wre are to embark upon something of this kind I believe the sooner we recognize these factors and give them thought and study, the better it will be. It appears to me that we are now just about in the position in which the Minister of Veterans Affairs is, when he said that he is both for public ownership and for private enterprise. No one can find any grave fault with that statement, if he can work it out in practice. But when we do come to work it out in practice, will it give the individual an equal opportunity against equal odds? And the odds at the present time are in favour of those who do not have to bear a share of the nation's costs.

Mr. Speaker, time is short, and I have only a few words to say. I rise to-night for only two or three reasons. In the first place, my honourable and jovial friend, the Minister of Veterans

Government Companies
Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) said this afternoon that the speech made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) was most stupid and fascist-

speechtext:
I thought he said fascist, and I take exception to that. I must apologize if the minister did not say "fascist".
I thought my colleague from Vancouver South made a well-reasoned, plain and well-ordered speech, and my only complaint is as to the fact that the Minister of Veterans Affairs described the speech as stupid. After listening to him, the only conclusion I must come to is that the minister is much more stupid than the hon. member for Vancouver South.
Replying to the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser), the minister said that the bill did not allow the setting up of crown companies. Of course it does; at least as I see it it does. How can you run a company without getting money for it? That is what this bill does. It says that any of these companies may be formed under part I of the Companies Act. They can get money from this measure, up to a million dollars.
So that the minister can go on and on and on, creating company after company, without coming to parliament at all. He has the money for it right there; only it is just a million for each company. But he can have as many millions as he likes by creating companies.
I object to the bill because it is the inalienable right of a member of the House of Commons, one which dates back to the times of Charles II, to take one's grievance to the foot of the throne. Since that time a member of the House of Commons has been given that right. For instance, that is what we do when we pass the estimates, the current issue of which I hold in my hand. Why not have many more companies? For instance, let us look into these estimates and turn first to the Department of Agriculture. Why not have a company to control the experimental farm service? Had we such a company, the ministry would not have to come to parliament at all; the minister would just take the money.
Then, let us turn to the insurance branch. Let us have a little company for that branch. I could gQ on. We are keenly interested in this, because the minister says that these statements of the companies are brought down every year. I have not yet seen a statement of Wartime Housing Limited, nor do I know if one has ever been published. Of course we shall be told that everything is all right, and that we are doing it for a purpose. I do not know whether they operate at a profit or a loss.
Speaking about companies, the minister said that the system of bookkeeping was inadequate. Well, I have sat in the house for almost eleven years, and I have not yet found out whether the Post Office Department makes a profit or a loss. Money seems to go in one way and out the other. I do not know just how it is done.
Then, let us go on, because there is more here. For instance, as I have said, we shall have a little company to operate the post office, others to operate other departments. If we did, then they would not have to come to parliament for money, because they would simply get $500,000 to begin and another $500,000; that would be a million dollars between the two parts of the bill. Of course, that is just a start. When we get along a little farther they will be more ambitious; and when they find it so easy to get money in that way, without any kick from members, without any criticism on the estimates, they would just go on forming more companies.
I doubt if the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) would ever ask for a company to run his show, although I do not know about some of the other ministers. You see, first of all, we have ministers; then we have parliamentary assistants, and now the job is getting so big we are going to have boards of directors for these companies. Indeed, after a while we shall have more people directing companies than are employed by them.
I do not think we are far apart in this matter. The hon. member for Vancouver South put it plainly when he said that if the minister wishes to incorporate a company he should put it in the bill. Let him come to parliament with a separate bill for each company, in the regular way. What objection could there be to that? We could have discussion; it would always be out in the open, and no one would be subject to criticism. Then, too, we would be preserving our rights as members of the House of Commons.
I, for one, do not intend to give up my right to criticize when the government asks for money. That is a most precious right. We relinquished that right to a certain extent during the war, because at many times in those years we were very careful about our criticism of the government, and the government knows that very well. We in the opposition had to be careful of what we did, and even then we were called saboteurs of the war effort because sometimes we criticized what the government was doing.
On motion of Mr. Ross (St. Paul's) the debate was adjourned.
